cards.text: Friend, this one's heavy, so pull up a stool. Babylon's army has burned Jerusalem and broken down her walls (Jeremiah 52:13-14). Now a poet looks at the city and cries, "How lonely lies the city, once so full of people!"

cards.question: Everything has flipped. She was great among the nations, and now she's a widow. And "The princess of the provinces has become a ___."

cards.text: Night falls, and she weeps aloud with tears upon her cheeks. She had lovers and friends, so where IS everybody?

cards.question: Jerusalem's friends are nowhere to be found. What does the poet say they have become?
Out of all her lovers, at least one comes to comfort Jerusalem.

cards.text: Judah has gone into exile, under affliction and harsh slavery. All her pursuers have caught up with her in the middle of her distress.

cards.question: Judah is in exile now, living among the nations. What does she find there?

cards.text: Even the roads to Zion mourn, because no one comes to her appointed feasts. Her gates are deserted, her priests groan and her maidens grieve.

cards.question: Jerusalem's foes have become her masters. The poet says the LORD has brought her this grief. Because of what?

cards.text: Her children have gone away as captives before the enemy. All the splendor has departed from the Daughter of Zion.

cards.question: The poet says Jerusalem's princes are like deer that find no pasture. What happens when the hunter comes?

cards.text: In her wandering, Jerusalem remembers all the treasures that were hers in days of old. I did that in the junk drawer, friend, except my good old days were a COUNTER.

cards.question: When Jerusalem's people fell into enemy hands, no help came. The poet says her enemies looked away in shame.

cards.text: The poet doesn't soften it: Jerusalem has sinned greatly. Everyone who honored her now despises her, and she groans and turns away.

cards.question: Her uncleanness stains her skirts. The poet says Jerusalem saw her downfall coming a long way off.
There's no one to comfort her. Then Jerusalem herself cries out for the first time. Who does she ask to look on her affliction?

cards.text: The adversary seizes all her treasures. And she has seen the nations walk into her sanctuary.

cards.question: The nations entered Jerusalem's sanctuary. They were the very ones God had ___ to enter His assembly.

cards.text: All her people groan as they search for bread. Then Jerusalem cries out again: "Look, O LORD, and consider, for I have become despised."

cards.question: To keep themselves alive, Jerusalem's people trade their treasures for food.

cards.text: Up to now the poet's been doing most of the talking. Now Jerusalem grabs the mic and calls out to everyone on the road: "Is this nothing to you, all you who pass by?"

cards.question: Jerusalem tells everyone passing by to look around and see. What does she want to know?

answers.text: If any sorrow is like hers

cards.question: Jerusalem says the LORD made her suffer on the day of His fierce anger.

cards.text: She paints her pain in pictures, one after another. He sent fire from on high that overpowered her bones, and He spread a net for her feet.

cards.question: The net the Lord spreads for Jerusalem's feet carries her safely home.

cards.text: Then Jerusalem pictures her sins a new way: they're bound into a yoke, knit together by His hand.

cards.question: Jerusalem says her transgressions are bound into a yoke, and they are "draped over my ___"

cards.text: The Lord has broken her strength and handed her over to those she cannot withstand. He rejects her mighty men and summons an army to crush her young warriors.

cards.question: The Lord has summoned an army against Jerusalem. What does she say He trampled the Virgin Daughter of Judah like?

cards.text: She weeps, and her children are destitute because the enemy has prevailed. Then the poet's voice comes back: Zion stretches out her hands, but there is no one to comfort her.

cards.question: The poet says the LORD has decreed something against Jacob. What is it?
Jerusalem speaks again: "The LORD is ___, yet I ___ against His command."

cards.text: She calls on all people to look upon her suffering, because her young men and maidens have gone into captivity. She called out to her lovers too.

cards.question: When Jerusalem called out to her lovers, they came running to help her.

cards.text: Her priests and elders died in the city while they searched for food to keep themselves alive. Then she turns to the LORD: "See, O LORD, how distressed I am!"

cards.question: Jerusalem says she is churning within and her heart is pounding. What reason does she give?

cards.text: Outside, the sword bereaves, and inside, there is death. People have heard her groaning, but no one comes to comfort her.

cards.question: Jerusalem's enemies hear about her trouble, and they are glad that the LORD caused it.
Jerusalem asks the LORD to bring the day He has announced and to deal with her enemies. How does she ask Him to deal with them?

answers.text: As He has dealt with her

cards.text: And the poem ends right where her heart is: "For my groans are many, and my heart is faint."

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 2 quotes "The princess of the provinces has become a ___.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 7 quotes "draped over my ___", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 12 quotes "The LORD is ___, yet I ___ against His command.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The setup line "She had lovers and friends, so where IS everybody?" already tells the baker that nobody showed up. That gives away card 5, which asks whether at least one of her lovers comes to comfort her.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The question says Jerusalem's friends "are nowhere to be found." Lamentations 1:2 says they have betrayed her and become her enemies. It never says they are absent or missing.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Most of the story cards in this stop (cards 4, 6, 8, 10, 13, 15 and 17) are plain paraphrase with no reaction, comparison or fatherly aside from Papa Dorin. Only card 1 ("grabs the mic") and card 20 carry any of his voice. A lament can hold a quieter tone, but these cards read as stripped-down summary.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess the exact image the verse uses for the trampling (grapes, grain or clay). "Trampled" fits all three, so the baker can't reason their way to the answer. This is the same kind of detail-guess as the Psalm 23 oil example the doc marks as bad.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: "Jacob" appears for the first time in this card. Nothing tells the baker who Jacob is, and here the name stands for the people, not the man.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The wrong answers for the second blank don't fit the sentence. "I listened against His command" and "I prayed against His command" don't read naturally, so "rebelled" stands out as the only word that works.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: The card says Jerusalem calls on all people to look upon her suffering "because" her young men and maidens have gone into captivity. Lamentations 1:18 sets the two lines side by side but never links them with a reason.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.
